title: AI Can (Finally!) Create High-Quality Maths Diagrams
author: Barton, Craig
summary: For two years, AI models could generate high-quality maths resources for Number and Algebra but failed badly at diagrams: triangles with angles not summing to 180 degrees, pie charts with overlapping segments, bar charts with bars hovering above the axis. The release of Claude Opus 4.7 changed this: the model now generates geometrically accurate, proportionally sensible diagrams for angle facts, Pythagoras, trigonometry, bar charts, pie charts, and pictograms on the first or second attempt, and can generalize reliably across ten or more variations. This has two significant implications for educators. First, teachers can now generate bespoke diagram-heavy practice sets for any geometry or statistics topic in seconds, filling a gap that previously made those sections sparse in AI-generated resource bundles. Second, AI tutors that were blocked from adapting geometric content to a student's specific conceptual gaps can now serve up carefully varied diagrams -- varying base, orientation, label placement, or units -- in the way a skilled human practitioner would. The author notes that high-quality diagram generation requires access to the latest frontier models, which cost approximately 20 GBP per month at minimum and more for production volume, a genuine equity consideration for resource-constrained teachers.
points: * The Achilles heel of AI maths resource generation -- diagrams -- has been overcome: Claude Opus 4.7 produces geometrically accurate, proportionally correct diagrams reliably on the first or second prompt. * AI tutors can now vary geometric diagrams the way a skilled teacher would -- changing only one variable at a time -- enabling high-quality adaptive practice for geometry topics that were previously inaccessible. * Teachers can now generate complete, A4-formatted, sensibly scaled geometry worksheets with answer spaces in seconds, replacing work that previously took an hour in Word. * The quality improvement is model-specific: free or older models still fail badly at diagrams; access to frontier models requires paid subscriptions that may create equity barriers. * The diagram ceiling was a hard constraint on AI tutor impact; lifting it opens the possibility of genuinely adaptive geometric practice, not just increased practice volume.
quotes: The second you asked it to draw a diagram, things fell apart. Triangles with angles that did not add up to 180. Pie charts where the segments overlapped. Bar charts where the bars hovered above the axis.

When I asked it to draw geometry problems involving angles, it was nailing them first time. And -- crucially for me -- it could generalise. Generate ten of them, vary the angles, change the orientation, all of them correct.

Imagine a student is stuck on the area of a triangle. The AI tutor could now serve up triangles, carefully varied. Just change the base -- keep everything else the same. Just rotate the triangle -- keep everything else the same.
The diagram problem was a real ceiling. And that ceiling has just been lifted.
